title: Zen Life, Enlightened Life, Sojun Mel Weitsman
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Andrea Thatch will share insights into the teachings of Sochun Mel Weizmann, a renowned Zen master who emphasized cultivating awareness and acceptance in everyday life. According to Mel's approach, enlightenment is not something separate from our daily experiences, but rather an authentic expression that arises when we let go of preconceptions and oppositions. By practicing Zazen and being present to the moment, one can develop stability and transcend their ideas about it, allowing for a more genuine experience of enlightenment in daily life.

sentences.text: So, Andrea does not need much of an introduction for most of us here.
Dragon Heart Ryushin Andrea Thach will tell us today about Zen life, enlightened life, the teaching of Sojun Mel Weitsman.
Like I said before, many of us will remember Andrea, who practiced with the Red Cedar Zen community in Bellingham from 2015 to 2019.
And then she left us and went back to Berkeley.
Her practice began much sooner than that.
She started practicing in 1994, and she was ordained in 2005 and received Dharma transmission from her teacher, Sojun Mel Weitsman.
So, thank you very much for coming and giving a talk.
Thank you.
Before I thank you all, we do the opening chant.
*An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect Dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
So, good morning, everyone.
It's so wonderful to see familiar faces, Talus with your hair shorter than I think I've ever seen it, and some new faces as well.
It's terrific to be here, and I can't help but evoke the feeling of the Red Cedar Zendo, where so many of you practiced for so many years and felt like a special home for a while.
So I'm delighted to be here for Zen Alive.
When Chris told me that the topic for the year was going to be enlightenment, I thought about that.
And that invite came around the same time that my teacher, my transmitting and ordaining teacher, was dying of cancer.
I don't know how many of you are aware of who Sojun Mel Weitsman was, but I wanted to have the opportunity to talk a little bit about his teachings on enlightenment.

I'll start by saying that when that idea came to my mind, I asked some of the other senior students, long-term practitioners at Berkeley Zen Center: do you know any talks that Mel gave on enlightenment, or what do you think he would say about it?
Almost to a person they said, "Oh, he never talked about that."
But actually, when I did some searches and looked through some of the old lectures, I think just about everything he talked about was enlightenment.
So we're going to open that up a little bit.
Sojun Weitsman was 91 when he died.
He was the transmitting teacher for 30 different teachers.
One of the early ones was Nomon's teacher, Norman Fischer, who many of you have studied with.
So his thumbprints are well over the Shunryu Suzuki lineage in this country.
I had the great honor to take care of him for the last months of his death, and that really informed some of my thinking about what I wanted to say today.
He was, in a very quiet way, very well known.
As I said, he had many, many transmitted students.
He also was one of the people who was involved in starting the Soto Zen Buddhist Association in America.
He was foundational in developing bridges between Japan and America as we were establishing our own lineage in our American way here.
He was one of the founding members of the American Zen Teachers Association that brought together Rinzai and Soto teachers.
So he had stature among his peers, although I don't think he was particularly well known.
The truth is he was also abbot at San Francisco Zen Center, and for almost 35 years, 45 years, he was abbot at Berkeley Zen Center.
Of all the disciples of Suzuki Roshi, of which there were many, he felt to be the one who most understood and embodied Suzuki Roshi's teachings.
Suzuki Roshi was the person who brought Zen to America in the current forms that we're all used to.
They're the forms that were transmitted through San Francisco Zen Center on to Norman, on to Norman and to you.
Mel didn't really stand out.
He wasn't very flashy, and he didn't make much of a splash in the Zen world larger than Berkeley and the wider Bay Area.

I wanted to say a little bit about his history, to give you a sense of how he lived his life and who he was as a person, to help you understand what he would say and why people didn't think he talked about enlightenment so much.
Mel came to Zen a little bit later; he was in his late 30s.
He had been, among other things, a cab driver and a boat painter.
He grew up in a poor Depression household.
He was born in '29 and didn't go to college.
He just went right out into the world.
He seemed like kind of an unlikely, plain fellow.

If you think about it, there are lots of stories of Mel as a cab driver in San Francisco, making his fare, getting to the place for the person who arrived, and sitting in the car and talking with them for some time.
Already, even at that point before he came to Zen, he was interested in people, interested in what made them up, and there for them.
So in the San Francisco Zen circles he seemed rather like a dumb guy, of all the people who were around Suzuki Roshi.
He was the one who wasn't so scholarly, didn't seem to relate to the sutras that well, and didn't really stand out.
The truth is he had an interesting background.
He studied painting with Clifford Still.

If any of you know abstraction, someone's raising their hand, if anyone knows about abstract expressionism in post-World War Two: Clifford Still was one of the founders of that, and Mel was actually a very accomplished painter.
His career was beginning to take off before he fell into Zen.
Like many of us, there was something that he recognized was missing.
He was open at a time when something was happening in San Francisco, something that was happening in the art community.
There's an early story of him going to sit his first sesshin.
Some of the kind of beat people and poets, the crowd that he was around, found this little Japanese man in Japantown.
They were going to sit zazen with him.
It was kind of a novelty, it was interesting, it felt like it was alive.
And he went to sit his first sesshin.
It was really hard.
You can relate to that.
It was really hard: his knees hurt, his ankles hurt.
He was incredibly restless.
I don't know if it was on that one day or if it was a multi-day sesshin, but at one point he just got up and left, during a period of kinhin, and he was out of there.
He went out and walked down to the Embarcadero in San Francisco, and walked around and walked around.
And he came back.
He realized that there was nothing else that he wanted to do.
There was nothing else that called his life or was important to him besides sitting Zen.
So that was really the beginning.
He had found himself.
He had immediate affinity with Suzuki Roshi.
He felt something about his style that was very intuitive.
Suzuki Roshi also didn't seem like he was a, in a way, very bright or very showy.

His early lectures, I understand, for the first several years, weren't really all that terrific, not just because he didn't speak English well and there was no one who could translate fluently for him.
But there was something about being around him that Mel understood.
He understood intuitively what Suzuki Roshi was transmitting, what Zen was.
And that's what I'm getting to hear him talking about: his enlightenment.
All those years he was a lay practitioner.
He used to go and sit zazen in San Francisco in the early morning hours, and he'd always wear the same sweater.
Same sweater with holes in it.
You can imagine the starving artist, and he had patches everywhere.
And one morning Suzuki Roshi took it and touched it and said, "That's your robe.
That's your robe."
And maybe a few years later, he and Mel were practicing together, doing something, and Suzuki Roshi said to him, "I'd like you to join our order."
What he was saying is, I'd like you to ordain as a priest.
Mel was one of the first five.
And he sent him off to Berkeley.
Eventually he said, "I'd like you to find a place in Berkeley and make a place where people can sit.
Be the caretaker."
Mel said, "I always felt like I was the caretaker there."
And Suzuki Roshi would come on Monday mornings to the attic of this old Victorian house, where we had to duck to get in, to be able to go in and sit zazen.
Slowly, over time, he had been ordained.
He finally received Dharma transmission after Suzuki Roshi died, and wasn't installed as Abbott until 21 years after the doors of Berkeley Zen Center first opened.
He wasn't pushing.
He wasn't trying to make anything happen.
He wasn't looking for anything.
Very organic.
In fact, in the first years after BCC had moved to its current site, about a mile away, there was a little garden next door, and he was always gardening.
He felt like cultivating a Zen community was rather like cultivating a garden.
And in it was a one-room schoolhouse, which was the Zendo.
His idea of the one-room schoolhouse is that everyone would practice together, and everyone would support everyone else, no matter what their experience or training was.
Everyone was teaching everyone, both equally, and based on their experience.
So that's how Berkeley Zen Center came to be, and something of Mel's background.
So I want to talk about Mel's enlightenment, if you will, or his teaching of his enlightenment as part of everyday life.
You already get a little flavor of that, don't you?
It wasn't about rituals and bells and whistles and fancy lectures, although he was an excellent lecturer.
It was really about a kind of cultivation and awareness.
We usually think of enlightenment as something really exalted, where we transcend our usual ways of being.
And maybe once you've had it, you can't really go back to the way it was before.
I don't think Mel really thought that way, or at least that was not at all his emphasis, which is why folks would say he didn't really talk about it.
So I'd say yes and no.
I think Mel would say, rather like Buddha nature, it's not that you have it or you don't have it, but rather you be it, or you exhibit it.
As far as our sort of Zen school of thinking goes, we all are completely Buddha nature.
Sometimes we're not as in touch with that in ourselves, and usually that's the clouding of our own mind.
Likewise, our expression of that, which is enlightened activity, is always there and always available.
That's really the key to Sojun, and I think Suzuki Roshi's understanding.
In the wake of Sojun's death, we've all been revisiting his life and his teachings, and we've all been reading what he's written.
The more I do it, the closer I see he is to Suzuki Roshi, and in his manifestations a lot of the words and phrases he used are exactly the same.
So there's a delusion within enlightenment and enlightenment within delusion, which really means your everyday life has absolutely everything that it needs in order to manifest enlightenment.
It's not some state over there, or that you get to after 10 or 30 or 50 years of practice.
That's what he would say.
Suzuki Roshi said, "The ordinary way practiced thoroughly is enlightenment."
Let me talk a little bit about what that means, to practice thoroughly: to leave nothing out, to include everything.
That includes those things, either within yourself, in your mind, in my mind, or out there, that we think are like, "Got to get rid of that, got to wash that clean."
Oh no, no, no, no, not that, that can't be.
So to practice thoroughly means to digest it thoroughly, to not be pulled around by it.
You accept it as part of the warts on your nose that you're born with: the form that you take, your height, your personality, your familial upbringing.
All of that is part of your enlightenment, even if some [unclear: "sums"] of it are an obstacle to you, or it seems like they're an obstacle.
It's common in our circles, Zen circles.
It was literally common in San Francisco Zen Center, in the years that I practiced there, that we'd say we raise the thought of enlightenment.
Well, that's the thought of Bodhicitta, right?
That's that first coming to practice and going, "Wow.
Yeah, that's it.
That's how I want to live.
That's what really matters to me."
That raising the thought of enlightenment seems kind of exalted, fancy.
I think of a little bit of the kind of atmosphere that I can imagine revolving around San Francisco Zen Center after Dick Baker died.
I mean after Suzuki Roshi died, and Dick Baker, who was entrepreneurial, really big, bright mind, big vision about what was going to happen.
There was Tassajara that was being developed, and he was the brains behind Green Gulch.
There was a bakery in San Francisco.
All of this bigness: that's kind of raising the thought of enlightenment, something big and grand.
And so Jim just enjoyed the practice.
He didn't try to raise the thought of enlightenment.
The atmosphere of practice itself was just very compelling, and the most vital part of practice was to be able to deal with difficulty.
So Jim just enjoyed the practice.
He didn't try to make anything.
He met it where it was.
And that's another quality of his expression of practice that I think all of us who were able to practice with him really value: whatever was happening right in front of you was the show.
It was the whole big deal, even though no one was making a big deal of it.
That's where the energy was, that's where the life was.
It wasn't supposed to look a particular way.
Whatever was there was it.
He said, "Our Zazen is our everyday life."
So, everyday life is in Zazen.
Everything shows up.
All the workings of our minds, our stories, our ideas, our feelings, everything is there: our past, our present, our ideas of the future.
It's all right there in our everyday life.
In Zazen we develop this stability to transcend our ideas about it.
He said don't stick to Zazen.
If after sesshin you feel happy to go home to your life, then you've really sat Zazen.
If you feel hesitant to leave, then you're stuck to Zazen.
When you practice moment after moment, then you just accept whatever is, and you won't have any complaints.
When you enjoy the practice, you don't have to stick to it.
You have a taste for it all the time.
It doesn't have to be in the monastery.
It doesn't have to be on the cushion.
We have to practice those ways.
Another one of Sojun's phrases that stands out to me is "enlightenment is an accident."
But by sitting Zazen and practicing, you become accident prone, by practicing sitting Zazen, by being willing to drop everything and be present to the moment.
We'll talk a little bit about this next.
Everything manifests itself.
You don't have to try and make it happen.
Sitting Zazen makes you prone to having your small mind take its proper place and your big mind manifest.
So I'm preparing for this.
I went over some of Mel's talks; there are a series of them that were given at Chapel Hill Zen Center at Pat Phelan's place.
Pat was one of his early Deshi, Dharma heirs, and for many years Mel would go and travel there to give a series of lectures and a kind of teaching Sojun.
So there are lectures on the Heart Sutra there.
There are lectures on the Genjokoan there, among other things that you'll find that he's spoken about.
When I think about enlightenment, everyday enlightenment, it really is Genjokoan.
For those of you who know Genjokoan, it's one of Dogen Zenji's, the founder of the Soto Zen schools, foundational teachings.
And it's really about manifesting enlightenment in our everyday life.

I took a portion of one of Mel's talks and I kind of extrapolated and added a few of my own comments, but I wanted to give you some of his words too, so that you could hear his voice and the way that he speaks about his understanding of coming to terms with his own difficulties and finding his way to a kind of freedom.
He wouldn't use that word, but he would like that word.
So Genjokoan, that's kind of pivotal, pithy.
I'm watching the time.
Chris or Desiree is the Tink, give me a hand if I'm talking too long.
So we can open it up, but I'll get going on this section of my talk.
So Genjokoan is probably all of the Shobogenzo revolves around Genjokoan.
The rest of the Shobogenzo is a commentary, if you will, on the enlightenment or the manifestation of our everyday life in practice.
And one of the pithy paragraphs in it, which many of us who've been around Zen for any time have as echoes within ourselves, is the paragraph:
*To study the Buddha way is to study the self.
To study the self is to forget the self.
To forget the self is to be enlightened by the 10,000 dharmas.
To be enlightened by the 10,000 dharmas is to free one's body and mind and those of others.
No trace of enlightenment remains, and the traceless element is continued forever.*
So those encouraging words for Sogen had echoes in Tozan's five ranks.
Tozan's five ranks are some idea about spiritual development that Tozan developed.
Mel didn't like the idea of a certain path or prescriptive way in practice, but you might say it's rather like reading anything or looking at a map.
It helps orient.
It helps orient you to some aspect of your experience as a practitioner.
So, to lightly make a reference to that, but to talk about each line by line with Mel's comments.
"To study the Buddha way is to study the self" might be likened to aspiration, that rousing the thought of enlightenment, or that feeling like I have nothing else to do.
I'm walking here in the Embarcadero, which has all the goodies in the world and all the sense delights and everything else, but there's really nothing here for me.
That recognition that there's something else that's missing, or something else that's outside of me that's important.
It may be called the shift to move from living by karma to living by vow, to orient to practice where everything starts to be about practice.
Do you remember, those of you who are here, I don't know all of you, but I think many of us have the experience when we first come to practice of recognizing: wow, this really fills a need.
This really addresses something within me that I couldn't have articulated, or maybe I hadn't found before.
It's kind of like that.
So practice becomes the compass by which you orient.
He manifested that as a teacher, I would say, also by not having personal aspirations.
He said, "A good teacher doesn't want anything for himself.
And a Zen person doesn't want anything for herself."
Meaning it's the beginning of orienting towards a less selfish life, to recognize that your life is part of something bigger.
He was a pretty important person.
He was Abbott of San Francisco Zen Center and Berkeley Zen Center, he helped found these organizations, he was well regarded internationally.
But people didn't know who he was.
His personal aspiration was to live by what he was called to do, and not in search for anything.

Something that really underscores that for me is, as he had cancer, and as he began, first as he got older, he went from being in the Zendo twice a day, five days a week, in our Saturday program, to taking a Thursday off.
And then occasionally to missing or sharing his teaching seat, because he used to give all the lectures.
We sat 5:40 Zazen in the morning, 5:40 in the afternoon.
He was always there.
For four days a week, and Saturdays, he was always there.
For sesshins, 5am, he was always there.
As he got older, he wasn't at the Zendo so very much.
He called it taking a sabbatical, his cancer sabbatical, to work on his writings.
And one day we were taking a walk.
Mel had a way of being very personal.
He was very, very intimate.
And he said, almost in this kind of confessional way, "I really enjoy sleeping in."
You know, he's 90.
"I really enjoy sleeping in."
And I went, oh.
And he said, "Yeah, I'm really a night owl.
I have a hard time getting in bed before midnight or one."
And I just had this, like, my head split open.
You mean for 50 years you've been getting up at 4:30 in the morning, or four?
He rode his bike from his house to the Zendo.
So you mean you're getting up at 4:15 every morning for all those years?
Not complaining.
You never knew that the guy didn't want to be up and be there.
You never knew what a struggle it was for him to give up his late night hours and his usual biological clock.
He just did it because that was just the practice.
I see echoes of the early echoes of his teacher's teaching.
There's a famous story of this, at San Francisco Zen Center, which is an old dorm for nuns, three flights of stairs up and down.
The tank and gets up to ring the bell to let people know to get up in the early morning hours.
And that usually goes off, I think, at, let's say, four a.m.
It gets up really early.
So the bell goes off and people start to get up and go down, and Suzuki Roshi gets dressed and goes down.
Some people start to realize that the [unclear: "tank and"] was an hour early, and they say, "Oh, we're an hour early.
Well, we'll go back to bed now."
So they went back to bed.
It was actually Mel who had rung the bell.
He had made the mistake.
He was correcting the mistake, so he went down there and sat because the bell had gone off.
When everyone came up an hour later, he got up off his seat after they were settled and took the kaisaku, the wake-up stick.
And he got every single one of them.
It's like, "What are you doing?
What are you doing?
The bell went off.
Come and sit zazen and keep the schedule."
This teacher really took that to heart, Mel really took that to heart all those years.
It lasted him all those years of getting up at four in the morning.
Maybe that's enough on that.
There are so many stories to tell you, so many encouragements to give you.
The second line of Genjokoan is "to study the self is to forget the self."
He calls that willing submission.
So there's aspiration and willing submission.
Willing submission means don't be self-centered.
*Let go of your resistances.
Let go of your self-centeredness.
Be Buddhist-centric instead of self-centric and putting oneself into the service of the Buddha Dharma.*
Let me say that again.
Those are his words.
*Let go of resistances.
Let go of self-centeredness.
Be Buddhist-centric instead of self-centric, or putting oneself in the service of the Buddha Dharma.
Living by vow instead of by karma.*
That's a little bit more than that.
I think living by vow instead of by karma is a great aspiration.
It's what I hold in my heart with practice: may I do this?
And then willing submission is that you really have to do this.
You really have to commit to it.
You really have to try hard to do this.
There was a time, like for many of us, that I think Mel got a little discouraged in practice.
Nothing seemed to be happening particularly.
And he went to Suzuki Roshi and he said, "Do you think I can do this?"
Or he said, "Do you think I should stop practicing?"
And Suzuki Roshi said, "Don't you think that this is difficult enough for you?
If you can find something more difficult, you should do that."
In other words, I think the key to living freely is to be willing to do what's the hardest for you.
And I don't mean like carrying 100 pounds up the side of a mountain, but I mean letting go of self-centeredness is darn difficult.
Really darn difficult.
And Zazen is one way of getting to see who we are in the midst of this.
Another dimension of this is to not create an opposition, which I think is a kind of prelude to the next part of Genjokoan.
He says, I think this is a key element of entering into the non-dual: that is, not setting up something outside of yourself.
To let go of one's self-centered ideas means to be open to other things.
It means to be open to other perspectives, other ideas, that the world doesn't revolve around me and my ideas of what it is or what it should be.
That it's unknowable because it's made of so many different perspectives.
Don't set up something outside of yourself, or kind of the training wheels for that.

He said, specifically thinking about being in pain when you sit in Zazen, that those really early experiences that we have when we sit, that most people experience when they sit, that it's just physically really difficult.
If you set up an opposition, there's me wanting my comfort and there's the pain that I wish would go away.
The experience of that usually is pretty painful.
It just doesn't go away in that paradigm.
But if you're willing to open to it, kind of to accept that that's the somatic experience in the moment, something else is possible.
But when there's just a duality between the two of them, just a tension, just a me versus you, then your tormentor doesn't go away.
It just becomes bigger and bigger.
Mel says of that time:
*None of us could sit very well.
It was hard on our ankle bones.
At that time, there were very few people who could sit well.
So we all had a very difficult time sitting.*
And that was very much the feeling.
It was really hard to do Zazen because we didn't have the experience.

I think nowadays we have the good fortune of having people who've been sitting at Red Cedar for 30 years, and they're pretty comfortable with their Zazen, so they're an encouragement for people who haven't been sitting as long.
So you kind of see, well, maybe it is possible to do this.
At least it could be encouraging.
But he says it was really hard to do Zazen, we didn't have the experience.
Suzuki Roshi used to urge me on: "Don't move."
Sometimes we'd be sitting and after about 40 minutes, just before it was time for the bell to ring, he would say, "We will sit ten minutes longer."
And so it was a wonderful surprise, a wonderful surprise.
You can tell he understood on some level.
The wonderful surprise that, "Oh, I have to figure my way out of this because I'm not going to get up and leave.
How am I going to do this now?"
That's the willing submission.
How am I going to do this now?
The next part of Genjokoan is "to forget the self is to be enlightened by the 10,000 things."
In my mind, this is what I usually think about as enlightenment.
Like I drop enough of my way of seeing things to have some experience of what we call emptiness.
Some experience that there's something else out there that's functioning, and I'm functioning in the midst of it.
We stop chasing after things and grasping after them with our ideas of wanting something from them.
We see them reveal themselves.
And that's how we set them free.
And we are set free.
His actual teaching of this was very good in words.
But I think the way he showed us was the way in which he handled things.
So the way in which, instead of moving the zabuton, the big black cushion on the floor, with his foot, he would pick it up and shift it.
You don't treat things like objects.
The way when you would hand him his teacup, if you were his Jisha, he would take it in both hands and you would feel the weight of his hands on the cup at the same time your hands were on the cup.
So there is a real connection between the two of you.
And at the altar, before he would do service, he was always rearranging things.
We used to joke about that: "Oh, Mel is nesting," or "Mel just has to have it be just so."
But actually he was feeling the harmony of the objects on the altar and harmonizing with them.
He was bringing them all into harmony at the altar.
That was so much about his teaching.
I can't say how incredible, how astute he was working with his students.
He observed each of us, and he had a pretty clear idea of what was going on.
He was ready with a turning word or often with an action, which again I think is an echo of how he apprenticed with his teacher.
I remember when I came back from Tassajara 20 years ago, all full of light and enthusiasm.
I was going around the Zendo after a Saturday program, fluffing all the cushions, the way you're supposed to fluff the [unclear: "capehawk"] on the zabuton and make it look nice.
I was doing that to each of them.
Mel circled back around when he was done bowing everyone out.
When people walked out of the Zendo door he would wait and bow to everyone.
He was done, he circled back around, and he noticed my energy doing that.
He got down on his knees next to me, took the zabuton, positioned it for me and showed me.
It was a body-to-body kind of transmission of not treating things like objects, allowing myself to interact with it.
I could give you many more examples of that.
That's one.
He says the humility is to know who you are.
That means neither too big nor too small.
You know your proper place, your proper functioning with things.
So when you know your proper functioning, you don't have to elevate yourself.
You don't put yourself down falsely.
You just fit in.
You just harmonize with those things.
This is one of my favorite lines in the Genjokoan: *to find your place right where you are actualizes the fundamental point.* That's what actualizes enlightenment, if you will.
*Fish swim the water and never reach the end of the water.* You're always in your right place.
If you're being a fish, you're always in your right place in the water, no matter where in the water you are.
There are two more lines to Genjokoan.
I think I'll bypass the rest of what I was going to say so we can talk a little bit.
So, to be enlightened, line four, he calls combined virtue or collective achievement.
The fourth sentence of Dogen is *to be enlightened by the 10,000 Dharmas is to free one's body and mind and those of others.* So our work is actually to benefit not only ourselves but others as well.
This is what Tozan calls combined virtue or collective achievement.
It's characterized by the Samadhi of receiving and the Samadhi of giving.
Samadhi: open, deep, receptive presence without an abiding self.
Jijyu Samadhi is self-joyous or self-fulfilling Samadhi.
Taijijyu Samadhi is others' fulfillment.
Jijyu means that you receive and enjoy the light of your own true nature, your essence of mind.
Essence of mind was a favorite reference of Sogen's.
It's from the Platform Sutra of Huineng.
It might be thought of as the bright clarity of light, the bright light of clarity before conceptualization, is how I think about it.
Taijijyu means that you use what you receive to help bring others into realization.
We don't use our realization to help bring forth the light in others.
It will not sustain itself.
So one is turning the light inward to receive and turning to illuminate in others.
We're strobe lights shining in all different directions around.
The absolute, everything as it is, and the relative world of duality, [unclear: "the rules don't harm things"].
The third side is to go beyond both sides to see one within the other, as if they're the same, neither is separate.
The oneness of duality and the duality of oneness was Dogen and Sogen's great teaching.
So, one more section.
Dogen's fifth sentence is *no trace of enlightenment remains, and this traceless enlightenment is continued forever.*
That's the final rank of Tozan.
It's called unity attained.
This is where one is no longer concerned about enlightenment or delusion.

It is when one embodies enlightenment and realization totally without the need to do anything special, but is ceaselessly working for the benefit of all beings without any special effort or even self-consciousness.
There is no clinging to enlightenment or delusion.
One has perfect freedom in all aspects of life.
It is the culmination of mind and body dropping.
Gosh, I could say so many things here.
But what just comes to my mind as I'm telling you this is when it was really clear that Mel's cancer had progressed.
He had lived with it for almost a year, a very serious form of cancer, so everyone was surprised.
